data.title: Pentagon revokes former Air Force secretary's access to classified information
data.description:
The Pentagon revoked former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall’s eligibility for access to classified information, accusing him of “unauthorized disclosure of classified information regarding Air Force One’s capabilities” to a news outlet, it announced Friday evening. 

Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said the Defense Department (DOD) also yanked Kendall’s “ability to hold any sensitive position,” he wrote in an X post.

“Safeguarding classified information is a non-negotiable duty,” Parnell added. “Those who violate that trust forfeit the privilege of access and any role requiring it.” 

Kendall did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

Kendall, a trained lawyer and engineer, served as the Air Force secretary from 2021 to 2025 during the Biden administration and spent decades in national security roles prior. He is currently a senior fellow at the left-leaning Center for American progress.

The Pentagon’s claims come amid a broader crackdown on press freedom, most recently with the Trump administration subpoenaing reporters from The New York Times over their coverage of safety concerns with the new Air Force One converted from a gifted Qatari luxury jet.

The Times last month reported that the Secret Service advised President Trump not to leave a NATO Summit in Turkey on the Qatari-gifted plane, as it did not possess the same defensive countermeasures as the older Air Force One — including advanced antimissile capabilities.

Trump decided to fly out of Ankara on the older jet out of an abundance of caution for a potential threat from Iran. He denied that security concerns were the reason behind the decision.

The president was reportedly incensed with the reports, ordering a leak investigation that subpoenaed the Times’ reporters and had White House officials turn over their phones as part of the probe.

data.title: Army removes a top US general in Europe from command
data.description:
The U.S. Army removed a top general overseeing forces in Europe from command in recent days, close to two months before his time in the role is slated to end, two U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal personnel matters, told The Hill on Friday.

Lt. Gen. Charles Costanza was the commanding general of the Army’s V Corps, a forward-deployed corps headquartered at Fort Knox, Ky., and Camp Kościuszko, Poland.

When reached for comment, the Army confirmed to The Hill Costanza’s removal, adding the matter was “referred to the appropriate authority in accordance with Army regulations.”

Brig. Gen. John B. Mountford, deputy commanding general of readiness for V Corps, will serve as the acting commanding general, an Army spokesperson said. 

Maj. Gen. Thomas Feltey, who was nominated for promotion to lieutenant general last month, is to assume command of V Corps at Fort Knox in October. Feltey previously led 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, Texas. 

Costanza’s abrupt removal comes as more than two dozen senior military officers have been removed or sidelined under the Pentagon’s leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The shake-ups have impacted the Army as well, with Hegseth removing Army chief of staff Gen. Randy George and Gen. Chris Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa. 

But Costanza’s ouster was not political and was not done at the direction of Hegseth, two sources familiar with Costanza’s removal told The Hill. 

“Conduct that would get a commander relieved at any level,” one of the sources said.  

Previously, Costanza, who holds a master’s degree in military studies from American Military University, was the deputy commanding general of U.S. Army Europe – Africa. Before that post, he was the commander general of the 3rd Infantry Division at Fort Stewart, Ga.

Costanza’s removal was reported earlier by ABC News.

The Pentagon canceled the planned deployment of the Army’s 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division to Poland in May. The brigade is based at Fort Hood, Texas.

Later that month, President Trump announced that the U.S. would send 5,000 troops to Poland.

Poland’s Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said in June that the return of U.S. service members to the country will materialize in the “coming weeks.”

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, told The Hill in late July that the U.S. still hasn’t sent an Army brigade to Poland. 

“They’re sitting down,” Bacon said. “They’re trying to wait them out or something. I don’t know what they’re doing.”

The Big Story 

FDA’s food ingredient review rule is coming 

In his quest to overhaul the food system, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is poised to propose closing a loophole that allows food and dietary supplement companies to self-attest that new ingredients are safe. 

Associated Press

Last year, Kennedy directed the Food and Drug Administration to investigate revising its Substances Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) rule, which allows companies to bypass traditional government notification and review. 

The GRAS designation was intended to allow common food ingredients—like vinegar, flour, baking soda or standard spices—to bypass safety reviews and become available to all food manufacturers. 

But companies have been taking advantage after FDA created what is known as the “GRAS loophole,” allowing a company to self-certify its ingredients were GRAS, and then voluntarily inform the FDA that it had done so. 

FDA is expected to propose, as early as Monday, making notification of GRAS submissions mandatory for most substances.

 

The proposed rule cleared the White House regulatory review last week. 

“For far too long, ingredient manufacturers and sponsors have exploited a loophole that has allowed new ingredients and chemicals, often with unknown safety data, to be introduced into the U.S. food supply without notification to the FDA or the public,” Kennedy said in March 2025 when he directed FDA to revise the rule. 

The proposal represents a significant effort by the Trump administration to take a food safety goal championed by Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement and turn it into regulatory action. 

But there are going to be numerous hurdles to turning a proposal into final action, and food industry opposition is likely to be intense.

data.title: Trump administration targets Head Start for overhaul
data.description:
The Trump administration unveiled plans Thursday to overhaul the early education program Head Start for impoverished children.

The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) — called “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs” — from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) says it will “restore flexibility to programs to meet local needs, reduce regulatory burden and administrative costs.”

“We are removing unnecessary bureaucracy, strengthening nutrition and physical health, trusting parents and local communities, and opening Head Start to hundreds of thousands more children. That’s how we renew the promise of Head Start for the next generation,” said Kennedy in a press release accompanying the NPRM.

Head Start began in the 1960s to help fight against poverty and has received bipartisan support in Congress and presidential administrations over many years. The free, federally funded program for low-income families provides education for infants through preschoolers.

It currently serves roughly 700,000 children across the nation who are experiencing homelessness, in foster care or disabled.

The program is traditionally guided by its performance standards that outline every detail of the program including family engagement, faculty qualifications and more. 

The standards were last revised in August 2024 and the NPRM, if passed in its current form, would replace the more than 120-page document with around a dozen pages of rules. The new proposed rules would leave most of the specifics in the standards to state and local law while also requiring more documentation from families to enroll in the program, according to the Associated Press.

One potential rule from the NPRM would force programs across the country to deny enrollment to a child if documentation is not provided by the family to confirm the child’s age.

The overhaul would, according to the HHS, save the federal government $2.2 billion and preserve or expand 236,000 Head Start slots nationwide.

The Trump administration had attempted to eliminate the program in its White House budget request for the 2026 fiscal year. In the preliminary phase of the proposal, the program was reportedly eliminated outright.

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. testified before Congress that his agency will “preserve” Head Start. Congress approved a budget that gave roughly $12.4 billion to the program.

The public can comment on the NPRM for 60 days with the period elapsing on October 6.

data.title: Senate confirms 74 Trump nominees: Here are 5 notable ones
data.description:
The Senate confirmed dozens of President Trump’s nominees on Friday, the final day of session before the upper chamber of Congress broke for August recess. 

In a single 51-47 vote, senators voted to confirm a group of 74 executive nominees. 

The vote fell along party lines, with GOP Sen. Cynthia Lummis (Wy.) and Mitch McConnell (Ky.) not in attendance. 

Here’s what you need to know about six notable nominees confirmed under today’s vote:

FEMA Administrator

The Senate voted to confirm business executive Cameron Hamilton to lead the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) during a turbulent time at the agency.

Hamilton previously served as the acting leader of FEMA at the beginning of Trump’s second term. He was ousted after he contradicted Trump and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem by saying that the agency should not be eliminated. 

Hamilton told lawmakers during his June confirmation hearing that the agency should “seek to strike a new balance to encourage cost reasonableness and cost savings.”

TSA Administrator

David Cummins, a senior vice president of government services contractor Serco, will take the helm at the Transportation Security Administration after he was confirmed by the Senate on Friday. 

His appointment comes at a time when the Trump administration is pushing to downsize this federal agency and replace some of its airport services with private contractors. In April, the president proposed cutting over 9,400 workers and around $1.5 billion in funding from TSA. 

Cummins outlined his key objectives in this new role in a Friday press release from the agency, including “improving morale” at the agency, implementing new technology at TSA checkpoints, reducing travel wait times and protecting transportation networks from drone and cyber threats. 

“TSA will deliver on its role to secure the Golden Age of Travel the Trump administration has ushered in,” Cummins said in a statement. “We do not have to choose between a secure checkpoint, an efficient checkpoint, or an elevated experience.”

Commissioner of Labor Statistics

The Senate approved veteran economist Brett Matsumoto’s nomination as commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Matsumoto first joined the BLS in 2015 and most recently worked on the White House Council of Economic Advisors. 

His appointment follows Trump’s dismissal of former BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer last August over unsubstantiated accusations that the long-serving labor economist manipulated an unfavorable July 2025 employment report. 

Matsumoto assured lawmakers during his June confirmation hearing that he believed “strongly” in the bureau’s work “to produce objective quality measures.”

“It is important for the public to be confident that decisions at the BLS are being driven by science rather than politics,” he said at the time. 

Secretary of Labor

Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling will now oversee the department in a permanent capacity after the Senate confirmed him to a full-time post on Friday. 

Sonderling has served in an acting role since April 20, following the resignation of former Secretary Lori Chavez DeRemer amid an investigation into alleged misconduct by her and her husband. 

He previously served as DeRemer’s deputy for over a year. Under the first Trump administration, Sonderling was the administrator of the Labor Department’s Wage and Hour Division. 

Sonderling said in a June statement that he was “deeply grateful” for Trump’s endorsement of him for a full-term post. 

“Serving in both of President Trump’s Administrations has been the greatest honor of my life,” he wrote on social media. “If confirmed by the Senate, I look forward to continuing that service as Secretary of Labor and advancing the President’s agenda on behalf of America’s workers, families, unions, and job creators. 

Ambassador to Jamaica

The Senate also confirmed Kari Lake as the next U.S. ambassador to Jamaica, after the president nominated the head of the U.S. Agency for Global Media back in May. 

The former news anchor and Republican Arizona gubernatorial and Senate candidate has been a close ally of the Trump administration. She will replace Chargé d’Affaires Scott Renner, who has been serving as acting ambassador to the country since last January. 

Lake thanked the president for his nomination earlier this year in a social media post, saying she knows the country of Jamaica “very well” and that it is “full of incredible people.”

“If confirmed by the Senate, I look forward to strengthening the partnership between our nations, advancing America’s interests abroad, and building on the deep friendship shared by the American and Jamaican people,” she added.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin contributed reporting.

data.title: Trump urges GOP to keep Senate in session until college sports bill passes
data.description:
President Trump on Friday ramped up the pressure on Senate Republicans to cancel part of their August recess, this time urging embattled GOP senators to stay in Washington until they pass a bill to reform rules for compensating and recruiting college athletes.

The measure has been bogged down in the Senate, and the disagreement over the measure appears to be holding up a deal to speedily advance other priorities.

“THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT is a great Bill, and the Senate will hopefully stay in D.C. until it passes,” Trump declared on Truth Social.

“Without this Bill, millions of young Athletes will be hurt, programs will be canceled, Women’s and Olympic Sports will go away, the fans will be robbed, and Universities will go broke,” Trump warned.

The Senate Republican cloakroom on Friday circulated a “hotline” alert to gauge potential objections to the college sports bill, a bipartisan measure that was negotiated by Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

The measure would establish nationwide standards for name, image and likeness (NIL), transfers and eligibility for college sports.

Cruz is pushing for unanimous consent to vote on the bill before the Senate leaves for a five-week recess.

The “hotline” circulated by Senate GOP leaders proposed voting on a motion to proceed to the bill and, if it’s successful, a follow-up vote to pass the legislation at a 60-vote threshold.

But one senior Senate GOP aide said there are multiple objections to advancing the bill so quickly.

“It’s complicated, there are a lot of pieces to this. I’m okay with waiting,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), whose home state includes the SEC powerhouse the University of Georgia.

The Aflac Kickoff Game last month offered a major name, image and likeness deal with Auburn leading up to its game against Baylor on Sept. 5.

The SEC and Big Ten conferences initially opposed the Protect College Sports Act but recently issued a statement expressing support for the legislation after negotiating changes with the bill’s authors.

Some Republicans, including Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), have expressed concern the legislation as drafted could overturn laws passed in 27 states barring transgender athletes from women’s sports.

Trump on Friday insisted the bill would not override those state laws.

“Nobody has done more to protect Women Athletes than me — and this Bill CLEARLY protects the Laws in 27 States protecting Women’s Sports, and banning Men from Women’s Sports. Anyone who tells you differently is LYING! Stop grandstanding, and try getting this done,” Trump declared on Truth Social.

Trump had previously demanded that the Senate cancel its August recess to continue debating and voting on the SAVE America Act, which would require people to prove citizenship when registering to vote and require voters show photo identification in federal elections.

The president has also urged the Senate not to leave for the August recess before passing a budget resolution to set the state for passing a third reconciliation package to provide new funding for the Pentagon, struggling farmers and grants to states to adopt election reforms.

Thune has proposed voting on a motion to proceed to the budget resolution before senators leave town for the recess.

data.title: Alito to WSJ: 'Obviously I'm here for another term'
data.description:
Justice Samuel Alito shut down any notion he’s planning to imminently retire from the Supreme Court in an interview with The Wall Street Journal published Friday. 

It marks the justice’s first known comments on his future plans since NPR erroneously reported that the conservative jurist had announced his retirement on the final opinion day of the court’s term. 

“Obviously I’m here for another term,” Alito told the Journal’s opinion section. 

Alito has never publicly suggested he intends to retire, but NPR’s report came amid speculation that he may step aside so President Trump could nominate a replacement while Republicans hold a majority in the Senate. 

At 76, Alito is the court’s second-oldest justice, behind Justice Clarence Thomas, 78. But both are still younger than the most recent justices who’ve retired. 

Alito’s interview lands as the justice gears up to publish his first, full-length book in October as the court kicks off its next term. 

“It’s not pleasant, in the sense that it’s a reminder of mortality,” Alito said in the interview, in reference to the retirement rumors. “It’s like, what are those vultures doing up there? They are flying around. But it goes with life tenure.” 

The justice also pushed back on critics who’ve taken aim at him for dissenting in favor of Trump in recent major decisions on tariffs, birthright citizenship and the firing of a Federal Reserve governor. 

“I vote in every case the way I think the case should be decided. If that means a high correlation with what Trump wants, fine. If it means zero correlation with what Trump wants, fine as well,” Alito told the Journal. 

The justice said he wouldn’t decide a cases the other way simply so people would call him objective. He called that “absolutely wrong.” 

“There have been people who’ve recommended to me that I do that. I’m not going to do that,” he said in the interview.

data.title: Trump restarts effort to fire Fed's Lisa Cook: Reports
data.description:
President Trump is reportedly renewing his effort to boot Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook from her position, despite the Supreme Court thwarting his earlier attempt in June.

A letter from White House presidential aide Dan Scavino, dated Wednesday, said the president was “considering” removing her, according to a copy of the letter obtained by PBS NewsHour.

The letter was first reported by ABC News.

It said there was “sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements.”

It also asked her to “prove a written response with your explanation for your false statements and accompanying evidence,” within three weeks.

Trump first tried to fire Cook last August over accusations of mortgage fraud in an unprecedented move. It came after a referral from Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, who suggested Cook illegally designated properties she had in Michigan and Georgia as primary residences to receive better financing terms.

She fought the firing and pushed back on the allegations, arguing that it was spurred by Trump’s frustrations over the central bank not lowering the interest rates quickly enough.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that she can remain on the job as the case moves forward.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote at the time that Trump didn’t give Cook due process to contest the allegations, but also noted that whether she can removed “for cause will depend in part on the underlying facts.”

“In this opinion, we have not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards. Rather, we have simply addressed the parties’ arguments about the appropriate legal standards under which the facts must be evaluated,” he wrote.

In a statement, Cook’s legal team said they will fight “this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed.”

“These allegations are as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve,” the statement said. “No matter was President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent – there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. The Federal Reserve declined to comment.

data.title: Spokesman for Chuck Edwards blasts Ethics panel, report: 'Not driven by due process'
data.description:
Rep. Chuck Edwards’s (R-N.C.) spokesman Paul Shumaker slammed the House Ethics Committee panel that cited him for inappropriate behavior following Edwards dropping his reelection bid for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. 

In an appearance on PBS’s “State Lines,” Shumaker called out his issues with the House Ethics report that resulted in Edwards’s drop from the election.

“First of all, there was never a forward complaint lodged against Congressman Edwards. It was taken off. The committee chose to do the work based upon anonymous news sources and news stories that had been generated,” Shumaker said.

The report on Edwards, released Monday, recommended he be formally censured by the full House because he had violated “the spirit” of the chamber’s rules against sexual harassment and unwanted advances.

The Ethics Committee continued in the report that Edwards’s behavior with “two young staffers, repeatedly over a sustained period, was beyond inappropriate.”

Shumaker disagreed with this assessment and stated the committee gave “less than an adequate amount of time” to Edwards’s legal team to respond to the allegations.

Edwards’s attorney did formally respond over the weekend to the report, saying the recommendation for censure was based on “vague standards requiring credible behavior and adherence to the spirit of the Rules of the House” rather than rules violating sexual misconduct.

“The committee had already been in the field, polling on this issue and looking for other alternatives. So, you have a process that’s driven totally by politics, not driven by due process,” Shumaker added.

Shumaker confirmed that Republican leadership had asked Edwards to step down by Tuesday following the allegations. Edwards announced early Wednesday on social platform X he would drop his reelection bid but would complete his current term in the House.

“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” he wrote.

North Carolina Republicans have not announced his replacement that will appear on ballots in the general election.
